The great artificial intelligence debate of our time usually focuses on who will win the race for the most powerful model. A far more revealing question sits underneath the surface. Which country is building a healthier, more durable market structure around this technology? On that front, the evidence points in a surprising direction. China is playing a better long-term game, even though its stock market took a sharp hit first.

Wall Street loves a good American exceptionalism narrative. The story goes that the United States boasts the deepest capital markets, the most advanced chips, and a culture of relentless innovation that China simply cannot match. That story contains real truth, but it misses a crucial nuance. The United States has built a dangerously narrow AI ecosystem that depends on a handful of corporate giants. By contrast, China absorbed a severe financial shock and emerged with a strategy that prioritizes industrial diffusion and global market share over speculative stock prices.

Let us start with the American setup. The U.S. AI boom rests on a concentration of capital and corporate power that is unprecedented in modern financial history. A handful of hyperscalers, led by Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Meta, are pouring hundreds of billions of dollars into data centers and computing infrastructure.

Goldman Sachs estimates that the largest hyperscalers will spend nearly $800 billion on capital expenditures this year alone. Data shows that the “AI Big 10″s now account for roughly 42% of the entire S&P 500 market capitalization. This narrowness creates a fragile loop.

The equity market has become the broader economy’s growth engine. Rising AI profits lift share prices; higher share prices boost wealthy households’ spending power; and that spending keeps demand alive. This works beautifully as long as confidence holds, but it leaves the entire system vulnerable to a single point of failure. The top 10 S&P 500 stocks are the most concentrated they’ve been since 1965. Investors pay roughly 22 times forward earnings for the index, well above its long-term average, and AI-linked names trade at far richer multiples. When an index depends on a tiny group of companies to justify its valuation, the risk of a sudden repricing never disappears. It simply waits.

Now consider China’s path. The Chinese AI stock sector saw a sharp correction that wiped out roughly $480 billion. The STAR50 index, which tracks the country’s leading AI and semiconductor firms, plunged over 40% from its July peak. Even after that sell-off, the index traded at around 100 times trailing earnings, down from nearly 250 times. Retail investors fueled that rally with margin financing and short-term speculation. When sentiment shifted, the unwinding happened quickly. Beijing did not engineer that crash. No government deliberately vaporizes $500 billion in household wealth. The business model that triggered the correction reflects a deliberate and coherent strategic choice.

That choice centers on open-weight artificial intelligence. Labs such as DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot have released powerful models that anyone can download, modify, and run on their own servers. This approach contrasts with the closed-source, subscription-based models favored by OpenAI and Anthropic. The strategic logic is straightforward. If a developer in Nairobi, Lagos, or Jakarta can access a capable model from China for free, the pricing power of Western AI giants erodes.

Open-weight systems from China accounted for 17.1% of global AI model downloads through August 2025, edging out the U.S. share of 15.86%. On Hugging Face, the world’s leading open-source AI community, architectures from China captured 41% of all downloads by mid-2026. Alibaba’s Qwen ecosystem has birthed over 300,000 derivative models created by developers worldwide. Cumulative downloads of open-source large language models from China crossed 10 billion globally. These are not the metrics of a bubble. They reflect a platform strategy.

The Chinese government actively supports this diffusion. State-backed investors have even sold into domestic rallies to temper speculative excess, favoring long-term industrial utility over short-term financial mania. Beijing wants cheap, efficient AI embedded in manufacturing, logistics, and supply chains, not a bloated software stock bubble that enriches day traders while starving the real economy. China’s manufacturing base gives it an application advantage. The country accounts for roughly 30% of global manufacturing output, and that scale offers a ready testing ground for factory automation, robotics, and logistics software.

The short-term pain is real. Startups in China are bleeding cash as third-party cloud providers capture much of the end-user revenue. Z.ai’s share of its own model’s tokens that a major platform served plunged from 88% to 22% within 20 days of release, as rival hosts undercut its pricing. Financial returns for individual labs remain uncertain. Strategic returns for China’s broader economy and global influence are substantial.

The United States is not standing still on hardware. Washington continues to restrict China’s access to advanced chips, and those restrictions bite. Huawei plans to double production of its top-tier Ascend 910C chip to roughly 600,000 units in 2026, but Nvidia’s best chips still deliver around 4 times the computing power of Huawei’s best offerings. Bernstein estimates that China’s AI computing capacity stood at just 14% of America’s in 2025, and that gap will persist for years. China compensates for hardware weakness with software strength and industrial scale. The country is aggressively replacing foreign chips with domestic alternatives and forcing state-funded data centers to transition to homegrown silicon. DeepSeek’s founder has argued that domestic AI chips lag the U.S. by only about 2 years. The core constraint is production capacity, not fundamental design capability.

The deeper divergence lies in global outreach. The United States ties AI exports, cloud access, and investment to political and security alignment. It builds walls around its technology and expects allies to operate within those walls. China courts the Global South with open-source technology transfers, digital infrastructure, and low-cost AI stacks. It does not demand political loyalty. It offers capability. For a developer in an emerging market who cannot afford an expensive subscription to a Western model, a free Chinese model that runs on local hardware isn’t a compromise. It is a lifeline. This inclusive approach builds grassroots adoption, and adoption creates dependency, standards, and long-term influence.

The American AI trade may not crash tomorrow. Corporate balance sheets are strong, and institutional capital moves more slowly than retail margin debt. The structural vulnerabilities are real, though. The U.S. market depends on a narrow group of companies to justify extraordinary valuations amid rising capital costs and uncertain returns.

China has already taken its medicine. It absorbed a sharp correction, disciplined speculative excess, and doubled down on a strategy that prioritizes widespread adoption over exclusive monetization. That strategy may not produce the strongest quarterly earnings reports. It may not generate the kind of stock market euphoria Silicon Valley celebrates. It builds something more durable. It builds an ecosystem. In the long run, ecosystems outlast bubbles.

Elon Musk wants Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) to add 10 gigawatts of AI computing power next year, built entirely on Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) hardware. Price that plan with Nvidia’s own numbers, and one customer’s shopping list comes out bigger than the chip giant’s entire expected growth.

That’s the math laid out by independent market-analysis newsletter StreetSignal, which argues one customer’s ambitions “could account for virtually all NVIDIA’s projected growth.” Here’s how.

Nvidia’s Giant Growth Target

In August, Nvidia forecast roughly 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, which ends in early 2028. It was the company’s first-ever year-ahead outlook, and analysts had expected 44%.

Nvidia called it a supply-constrained outlook: customers want more than it can make. By StreetSignal’s count, Wall Street now expects Nvidia’s annual sales to rise by about $292 billion, to roughly $703 billion.

Musk’s 10-Gigawatt Shopping List

AI data centers are sized by the electricity they draw, in gigawatts. More gigawatts means more chips.

SpaceX had 1.7 gigawatts at the end of September, and its finance chief expects 2.5 to 3 by year-end. On the Oct. 20 earnings call, Musk said he’d be “surprised if we brought on less than 13 gigawatts of compute” by the end of 2027. That’s roughly 10 more.

In August, Musk committed SpaceX to building exclusively on Nvidia. On Oct. 25, he said SpaceX had closed $40 billion of debt financing to buy GPUs.

Nvidia has said each gigawatt of its Vera Rubin systems represents about $40 billion of revenue opportunity, chips and networking included.

The Cautious Case: 7 Gigawatts

Here’s where that figure comes in. Every gigawatt of new computing SpaceX builds on Nvidia’s newest systems means roughly $40 billion of equipment the rockets-to-AI company must buy from the chip giant.

StreetSignal starts cautiously. It assumes SpaceX adds only 7 gigawatts of new computing in 2027, not the 10 Musk has projected. At $40 billion per gigawatt, the firm would need to buy about $280 billion of Nvidia equipment.

But Nvidia’s forecast is about growth, and SpaceX is already a big customer. So StreetSignal subtracts what it assumes Musk’s firm spends with the chipmaker this fiscal year, about $75 billion. That figure prices SpaceX’s roughly 3 gigawatts of year-end capacity at $25 billion per gigawatt, the rate for Nvidia’s current Blackwell systems.

Now, $280 billion minus $75 billion leaves $205 billion. That’s how much more SpaceX would spend with Nvidia in fiscal 2028, about 70% of the $292 billion in overall sales growth Wall Street expects for the semiconductor firm.

That would leave just $87 billion of growth for all of Nvidia’s other customers combined, including Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta and Oracle.

The Full Plan: 10 Gigawatts

Now assume SpaceX hits Musk’s full target of 10 new gigawatts in 2027. At $40 billion per gigawatt, the company would need to buy about $400 billion of Nvidia equipment.

Subtract the same $75 billion, and SpaceX’s spending with Nvidia would rise by $325 billion.

That’s $33 billion more than the $292 billion Wall Street expects Nvidia’s total sales to grow. For that forecast to hold, Nvidia’s other customers combined would have to cut their Nvidia purchases by $33 billion.

But Big Buyers Want More

They’re doing the opposite. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress said in the company’s August earnings call that the five biggest cloud companies are expected to lift capital spending from $800 billion this year to $1.3 trillion in 2027.

SpaceX also expects a big share of Nvidia’s limited supply. In the company’s August earnings call, Musk said, “our understanding with NVIDIA is that we will receive a very significant percent of their GPUs next year.”

Remember, Nvidia says it can’t make enough equipment to meet demand. If supply is that tight, StreetSignal argues, “somebody isn’t getting the GPUs they expect,” and that isn’t yet showing up in other companies’ forecasts.

StreetSignal’s Question for Wall Street

StreetSignal stresses it isn’t making a bearish call on Nvidia, and it flags two reasons its math is approximate.

First, some spending can be counted twice. StreetSignal points to Google, which rents computing power from SpaceX: SpaceX buys the Nvidia equipment, and Google pays SpaceX to use it. Nvidia makes that sale only once, so adding up every company’s AI spending plans can overstate how much Nvidia equipment is actually being bought.

Second, timing. Musk’s target counts computing switched on during calendar 2027, while Nvidia’s fiscal 2028 runs from roughly February 2027 to January 2028. And equipment is bought before it’s switched on.

StreetSignal’s bigger question is about Nvidia’s stock. By its count, Nvidia trades at about 13 times the profit analysts expect it to earn in fiscal 2028. A company forecasting 70% growth doesn’t usually trade that cheaply, StreetSignal says; such a price suggests “the best part of the cycle may already be behind it.”

“If all these assumptions are right, why are the stocks so cheap?” StreetSignal asks. It wants Wall Street analysts to reconcile the numbers rather than “simply raise another NVIDIA price target.”

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) heads into Monday’s fiscal fourth-quarter earnings report with Wall Street divided over whether its modest AI spending and strong cash flow make it Big Tech’s safest bet — or whether investors are paying too steep a price for that protection.

The iPhone maker is scheduled to report results after the U.S. market close on Nov. 2, with analysts expecting revenue of $113.39 billion and earnings of $1.99 per share.

Needham’s Martin Flags China, Memory Costs and iPhone Dependence

Needham analyst Laura Martin, who has a Hold rating on Apple, said the company is benefiting from its relatively light AI capital spending, strong free cash flow and continued shareholder returns.

Ahead of earnings, Martin told CNBC on Monday that she expected about $56 billion in iPhone revenue and roughly $31 billion in Services revenue, with Services carrying about a 75% margin.

However, she expected about 300 basis points of overall margin compression, citing sharply higher memory costs. Martin said investors should watch whether new CEO John Ternus raises iPhone prices or absorbs the cost pressure, which could slow EPS growth over time.

She also highlighted Apple’s 2.5 billion installed devices as a major competitive moat, but said Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and other AI players are trying to shift computing away from smartphones toward devices such as glasses.

Martin said the iPhone remains Apple’s anchor product and noted that roughly half of total revenue comes from it. She also identified China, which represents about 20% of iPhone sales, as an important risk to monitor.

See More: Top Value Stocks

Bernstein’s Newman Sees a Tech Safe Haven

Bernstein analyst Mark Newman told CNBC on Saturday that Apple has become a defensive safe haven within technology because it is not committing the roughly $100 billion-plus in annual AI capex that some peers are spending.

Newman pointed to Apple’s roughly $13 billion in capex last year and about $11 billion this year, along with growing earnings, free cash flow and continued share repurchases.

He said Apple therefore carries less downside exposure if the broader AI investment cycle weakens.

Newman also argued that Apple remains a key consumer gateway to AI because users are likely to access AI primarily through their phones.

He believes smartphones will remain relevant even as wearables develop because those devices still need processing power, battery capacity and a tethered computing platform.

Moffett Says Valuation Looks Stretched

MoffettNathanson analyst Craig Moffett also acknowledged Apple’s defensive appeal but said investors may already be paying too much for that safety.

Moffett told CNBC on Saturday that Apple trades at about 36 times forward earnings, implying an earnings yield of roughly 2.8%, which he viewed as a demanding valuation.

He also flagged rising memory costs as a potential pressure point. Moffett said Apple has already increased base-device prices by about $100, while U.S. wireless carriers have remained disciplined with promotions.

He believes Apple’s biggest competitive threat is not necessarily Android, but customers keeping their existing iPhones longer. Higher prices could encourage consumers to delay upgrades by several months, creating a headwind for future device demand.

Wall Street usually welcomes divided government. But veteran market strategist Ed Yardeni warns that a Democratic sweep in Tuesday’s midterm elections could deliver a “very cold shower” for stocks, even with Republicans retaining the White House.

Yardeni, president of Yardeni Research, told Bloomberg that growing political divisions could make it harder for Congress to respond to future economic crises.

Traders on Polymarket put the probability of Democrats capturing both the House and Senate at approximately 73%, with more than $52 million traded across the election market.

But Yardeni believes stock investors may not have fully priced in that possibility, noting that some remain skeptical of polls showing strong Democratic support.

Why Gridlock Could Hurt Stocks

“Usually the market loves gridlock, but in this situation we’re talking about much more partisanship,” Yardeni said.

Investors traditionally welcome divided government because it makes major policy changes harder to pass, reducing the risk of sudden changes to taxes and regulations.

Yardeni worries, however, that Washington could become so divided that lawmakers struggle to agree even when action is urgently needed.

He warned that future government shutdowns and disputes over the national debt could last considerably longer, potentially causing greater economic damage.

For Yardeni, the bigger concern is what happens if bond investors lose confidence in Washington’s ability to manage its finances.

Yardeni coined the term “bond vigilantes” in 1983 to describe investors who push back against excessive government borrowing by selling bonds.

If those investors demand higher yields, borrowing costs for businesses could rise, putting pressure on stocks. Congress might then need to agree on deficit reduction precisely when political divisions make compromise most difficult.

Yardeni Still Sees Buying Opportunities

Despite his warning, Yardeni isn’t predicting the end of the bull market.

In an October 29 Financial Times column, he argued that stock-market declines following the midterms could offer buying opportunities, supported by resilient economic growth and corporate earnings.

His view contrasts with that of Morgan Stanley strategist Mike Wilson, who sees the election as a potential clearing event for stocks, with the removal of political uncertainty potentially supporting a rally.

For investors in the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY), Yardeni’s warning is that even an election result widely anticipated by traders could introduce fresh risks if political gridlock fuels another fiscal confrontation.

Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) has reached a level of annual gross profit that took Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) more than three decades to achieve — and it has done so in just five years. The comparison captures the extraordinary speed of the AI startup’s rise.

But investors weighing its coming IPO will need to look beyond the headline number to understand what is powering the growth — and whether the economics can support a valuation that puts it in the same league as the biggest companies in the market.

Anthropic: A Five-Year Run to $40 Billion

Fiscal.ai’s Nov. 1 analysis found that 79 companies currently generate more than $40 billion in annual gross profit. Outside Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) and Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG), every company on its list took at least 20 years to reach that threshold. Nvidia needed 31 years, while Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) each took more than three decades. Anthropic, founded in 2021, got there in five.

This is annualized gross profit, not cumulative profit or net income. Fiscal.ai attributes the margin expansion to fixed per-token pricing and lower processing costs as hardware use and inference become more efficient. Gross margin moved from below zero to above 80% in less than two years, it said.

Read Also: Anthropic Pays 33% Above Market for AI Capacity

Enterprise Demand Is the Engine

Anthropic had more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000 annually as of Sept. 30, including more than 1,900 spending over $1 million. Net revenue retention reached approximately 900%, reflecting sharply higher spending by existing customers. More than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app such as Claude Code or Cowork, according to its IPO filing.

Anthropic reported $16.95 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 1,127% from a year earlier, in its Nov. 2 amended IPO filing. It has applied to list on Nasdaq under the proposed ticker ANT, bringing the fast-growing AI business closer to public-market investors.

The $2 Trillion Question

Anthropic’s growth invites a much bigger question: Could it eventually command a valuation approaching $2 trillion? That would put it in the territory of the world’s largest public companies, including Nvidia. Its rapid gross-profit expansion and enterprise adoption make the comparison worth considering, but reaching that scale would require sustaining growth while converting demand into durable cash generation.

The compute bill remains a major hurdle. Anthropic’s business depends on enormous investments in chips, data centers and cloud capacity. Its infrastructure commitments could absorb substantial cash even as revenue and gross margins expand.

Anthropic’s five-year sprint shows how quickly AI demand can create a major business. The $2 trillion question is whether it can turn that growth into the scale, profitability and cash flow required to join the market’s most valuable companies.

The risk of an artificial intelligence bubble bursting remains relatively low, but investors could be overlooking significant concentration risks in some of the most popular semiconductor ETFs, according to Tal Schwartz, founder of Ai Funds.

The firm’s recently unveiled AI Bubble Pop Index currently scores the risk at just 3 out of 20, based on Oct. 2 readings. However, Schwartz cautions that the index measures the broader market, not individual sectors.

“It doesn’t score sectors, so a low reading isn’t a clean bill of health for any of them,” he told Benzinga.

Read Also: Semiconductor Stocks Are Cheaper Than the S&P 500: Is It Time to Buy SOXX and SMH ETFs?

Nvidia Exposure Separates the Riskiest AI ETFs

Among major AI-related ETFs, the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) appears particularly vulnerable. When asked which, among the major ETFs investors use to play the AI theme, has the greatest vulnerability to an AI spending slowdown, Schwartz opined that it was SMH, due to its concentration.

Nvidia Corp (NASDAQ:NVDA) accounts for approximately 21% of its portfolio, while its top 10 holdings represent 69% of assets, according to Morningstar data.

By comparison, the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (NASDAQ:AIQ) holds approximately 90 stocks, with its top 10 accounting for around 33% and Nvidia representing less than 3%.

“The more a fund depends on one group of customers’ spending, the more a capex slowdown could hurt it,” Schwartz said.

The iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SOXX) also carries semiconductor exposure but is more evenly distributed, with Nvidia accounting for approximately 8%.

AI Spending Slowdown Could Hit Chipmakers Hard

A hypothetical 20% reduction in hyperscaler AI infrastructure spending over the next 12 months could put chip equipment makers, memory manufacturers, AI accelerators and networking suppliers under pressure.

“The suppliers whose revenue is that spending: chip equipment makers, memory, AI accelerators and networking, plus the optical and power names common in thematic funds. These companies carry high fixed costs, so a revenue dip tends to hit earnings harder, and their valuations assume years of growth," Schwartz explained.

“In the 2022 chip downturn, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 45% from its January high to its October low. The twist is that the hyperscalers themselves could hold up better, because spending less lifts their free cash flow,” he added, illustrating the sector’s vulnerability to spending cycles.

QQQ and SPY Also Carry Hidden AI Risks

At September-end, the top 10 stocks represented approximately 47% of the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) and 39% of the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY).

“The risk runs deeper than the weights. Nvidia sells to Microsoft Corp (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com, Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc (NASDAQ:GOOGL) and Meta Platforms, Inc (NASDAQ:META), which sit in the same funds, so one capex decision hits both sides,” Schwartz explained.

He added, “A cap-weighted index is static by design. It owns the most of whatever has already risen the most, and it rides every decline.”

Investors seeking to reduce concentration could consider the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), where technology accounts for approximately 16% of assets, compared with roughly 40% in SPY. However, equal weighting introduces greater exposure to banks, cyclicals and rate-sensitive stocks, Schwartz cautioned.

Why a Low Bubble Score Doesn’t Eliminate AI Risks

Three of the index’s 10 indicators currently carry yellow readings: AI-linked layoffs, China’s cheaper AI models and the yield curve. Big Tech capital expenditure already consumes approximately 80% of operating cash flow, with spending above 100% triggering a warning.

Schwartz also sees cheaper Chinese AI models threatening U.S. companies’ pricing power.

“In my view, it’s the chance that AI monetization disappoints because of Chinese ‘AI dumping,’ landing on a highly concentrated system,” he said.

Drawing parallels with Cisco Systems Inc (NASDAQ:CSCO) during the dot-com boom, Schwartz noted that even dominant technology suppliers can experience severe corrections.

“Cisco sold the routers that built the internet, Nvidia sells the chips that power AI, and both became the world’s most valuable company,” Schwartz said.

“On its way up, Cisco fell 38% in early 1997 on slowing sales and 37% in 1998 during the Russia/LTCM crisis. Yet it gained about 590% in the two years before its March 2000 peak. Nvidia lost $589 billion in one day on the DeepSeek scare in January 2025, then regained nearly all of it within weeks. Scares like these are swings. Cisco fell 89% by October 2002 only after its customers stopped buying,” he explained, noting that what ends a boom remained the same — customers reducing spending.

For ETF investors, his warning is particularly relevant: “Segments can swing hard inside a calm market. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index closed 20% below its June record in July, then fell 6.7% on October 22 alone.”

Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) and gold have "blown their tops," Bloomberg Intelligence strategist Mike McGlone said Monday, pointing to a stock market correction as the trigger that could drag both lower heading into Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Why McGlone Sees All Risk Assets Rolling Over Together

McGlone said on The Wolf Of All Streets podcast that Bitcoin, gold and silver have all pulled back to key support levels alongside a broader equity correction, calling it a Faustian bargain starting to unwind. 

A chart overlaying Bitcoin, gold and the S&P 500 (NYSE:SPY) on 50-week moving averages shows gold just beginning to roll over while Bitcoin already has, he said.

The real signal to watch, McGlone argued, is whether the S&P 500 closes lower this week, calling that outcome "the beginning of potentially the biggest reset of a lifetime." 

Correlations between gold, copper and the S&P 500 are running at record highs on a 50-week basis, he noted, meaning a stock pullback would likely drag commodities down rather than lift them as a safe haven.

Why McGlone Doesn’t Buy the ‘Markets Always Rally After Midterms’ Thesis

McGlone pushed back on the popular narrative that stocks reliably rise after midterm elections, warning that widespread consensus on any single outcome usually signals danger. 

He pointed to Bitcoin’s drop toward its 50-week moving average, a rolling housing market, and a sharp pullback in natural gas as signs a broader deflationary shift is underway.

Fellow guest Mario Nawfal pushed back on the crypto reaction specifically, noting Bitcoin only fell 4% to 5% during the week of the Binance hack, even as Intel dropped 30% and Alphabet fell 12%. 

He called that relative strength, not confirmation Bitcoin is rolling over.

Why the Debt Ceiling Could Hit Sooner Than Expected

Nawfal flagged the debt ceiling, set at $41.1 trillion against a national debt already above $40.5 trillion, as an underappreciated risk that could surface before year-end rather than its usual March timing. 

He compared the setup to 2011, when a debt ceiling standoff triggered a US credit downgrade from S&P and sent gold from $1,400 to $1,900.

Central banks have been accumulating gold at a record pace since 2022, Nawfal said, framing the metal as an emerging reserve asset rather than a traditional inflation hedge:

  • 2021 purchases: $26 billion
  • 2025 purchases: $96 billion

He also pointed to a Bank of England consultation paper exploring whether gold should be tokenized for financial market liquidity, calling it a sign institutional interest extends well beyond retail demand.

McGlone and Nawfal agreed the Fed faces a difficult choice heading into December, caught between inflation still above its 2% target and a stock market already showing signs of fatigue.

The story has been updated to include a comment from Meta and Ofcom.

On Friday, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), TikTok and X lost their legal challenge in London’s High Court against Ofcom over the British regulator’s requests for information under the Online Safety Act. This marks one of the first major legal tests of the U.K.’s newly introduced online safety framework.

UK Watchdog requested Data from Meta, TikTok and X

The case is among several legal challenges concerning provisions of the 2023 Online Safety Act, which imposes stricter requirements on platforms such as TikTok, X, Facebook and Instagram to protect users, particularly children, from harmful and illegal content.

In February, the U.K. media watchdog sent information requests to Meta, TikTok and X seeking detailed data on their content moderation practices, including the number of posts removed or restricted in visibility and the number of users exposed to harmful content.

The High Court, presided over by Justice Singh and Justice Collins Rice, ruled in Ofcom’s favor in the first judicial review cases examining the regulator’s authority to issue information notices under the Online Safety Act 2023.

The court said the charges were brought by operators of some of the U.K.’s most widely used social media platforms, including TikTok, X and WhatsApp.

Meta, TikTok and X argued that the information requests imposed unprecedented regulatory demands. X said complying with what it called “the most burdensome information request X has received from any regulator” would cost the company millions of pounds, the report added.

“We’re disappointed with the court’s decision. We and others across industry pursued this challenge because information-gathering of this scale goes beyond what is necessary or proportionate,” said a Meta spokesperson in an emailed statement to Benzinga. The spokesperson added that the company was committed to working with Ofcom and is reviewing the judgement in full.

TikTok told Reuters that it was reviewing the court’s ruling.

An Ofcom spokesperson told Benzinga that the agency welcomed the court’s decision “to dismiss the challenges brought by Meta, X and TikTok against our efforts to gather information from them.” The spokesperson added that gathering information from companies “is fundamental to our ability to do our job of assessing compliance with their duties,” and it will continue to use its powers to create a safer life online for people in the U.K.

TikTok and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ: SPCX) SpaceXAI, the parent of X, did not immediately respond to Benzinga’s request for comment.

Read Also: Meta Seeks About $95 Billion for AI Buildout as Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom Consider Investing in Their Own Customer

Meta Faces More Legal Battles

Friday’s High Court ruling marked a victory for Ofcom, although a potentially more consequential decision is still pending in a separate case brought by Meta over the regulator’s method of calculating fees and potential fines.

Meta is also contesting Ofcom’s classification of WhatsApp under the new regulatory framework, the report noted. Earlier this month, Ofcom said the tech giant is facing a probe into whether Instagram’s new Instants feature received adequate safety checks before its launch.

New Mexico also asked a judge to order Meta to pay between $35 billion and $40 billion after a jury found the company misled Facebook users about data privacy, access and content policies.

In August, Meta reached an $18 billion settlement with U.S. states and territories to resolve allegations that Facebook and Instagram caused harm to children.

Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) may be delivering strong hardware sales, but its strategy for the next wave of artificial intelligence is raising questions as personalized AI agents threaten to reshape how consumers interact with technology.

Gene Munster Sees AI Agents As Biggest Threat to Apple Ecosystem

Deepwater Asset Management managing partner Gene Munster believes personalized AI agents could become a major threat to Apple’s tightly integrated hardware and services ecosystem.

In a post on X, Munster said he was disappointed with CEO John Ternus’ responses to two questions about personalized agents during Apple’s earnings call.

Munster wanted Ternus to explain how Apple plans to position itself as AI agents transform consumer technology, rather than simply discuss improvements to Siri.

“It’s clear they don’t want to talk about personalized agents,” Munster wrote, calling them “the biggest risk to the Apple ecosystem.”

He estimated that around 20 million people currently use personalized agents, including Meta Platforms, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:META) Muse and Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) Grok Bot and predicted that usage could eventually reach billions of people daily.

Asked how these agents could affect Apple’s Services business, Ternus highlighted the company’s AI-powered Siri, saying there was room to expand its capabilities while maintaining user privacy and security.

On the second question, Ternus described the iPhone as a personal hub, highlighting Siri’s ability to securely access users’ information.

Ackman and Israel also noted, “By frontloading its compute investment, Meta has given itself the optionality to scale Muse to a billion or more users.”

Regarding MSFT, the executives stated, “Microsoft occupies an enviable position among the hyperscalers in having two large channels by which to monetize its compute.” They noted that “the narrative on the stock has shifted from the company being an AI laggard to an AI leader.”

‘Disconnected’ Valuations at Uber and Netflix

Beyond the hyperscalers, Ackman and Israel highlighted what they view as mispriced opportunities in other portfolio companies. Regarding Uber Technologies Inc. (NYSE:UBER), the executives noted the stock now trades at “its lowest valuation ever.”

They stated that investor concerns regarding autonomous vehicles are “increasingly disconnected from its strong business performance.” Ackman and Israel wrote that “the risk due to AVs is minimal,” and projected that Uber’s earnings per share will “compound at 25% or more for the foreseeable future.”

Addressing Netflix Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX), the letter noted that recent stock declines were driven by investor concerns over plateauing engagement. However, the executives argued that measuring engagement solely by watch time “overshadows the quality of that engagement, which is what ultimately drives the value proposition for Netflix subscribers.” Ackman and Israel concluded that the market “vastly undervalues the company’s growth profile and business quality.”

Hyperscalers Can Fund Most of the Buildout

The letter acknowledged concerns over how these companies will fund their infrastructure buildout. Ackman and Israel noted that the hyperscalers are “collectively expected to spend a little over $1 trillion on capital expenditures in 2027 based on consensus estimates.”

Tech Sell-Off and AI Demand

Climbing a Wall of Worry

During a CNBC appearance, anchor Joe Kernen noted the Nasdaq 100 lost 3% last week; Lee reaffirmed his conviction that “markets are going to exit the year strong.”

He acknowledged that underlying market performance has been a “real battle” due to investor nervousness surrounding war, AI spending, debt markets, the Federal Reserve, inflation, and the midterms.

However, Lee noted that “markets climb a wall of worry” and expects that resolving these issues will help “see money come off the sidelines.”

Midterms as a Clearing Event

Lee identified the upcoming midterm elections as a key “clearing event.” He explained that markets often prefer political gridlock because “you don’t have too much policy creep,” making the presidential veto highly important.

While investors worry about data center regulations if Democrats win Congress, Lee offered a “contrarian view that House Democrats will support AI post-midterms because it does bring money to their community,” adding that AI is “good for jobs and it’s good for the economy.”

Prediction Markets and Polling

Comparing the 2026 midterms to the 2024 cycle, Lee observed that current prediction markets and polls are “almost the same,” with both basically showing a Democratic sweep.

Consequently, he stated they are not “generating signal on the margin.” Because the prediction platforms and polling data are so heavily aligned, Lee concluded that “the bigger surprise would be Republicans doing better.” However, he noted hearing that Texas could emerge as a state where Republicans fare better than expected.

Elon Musk argued late on Monday that cooling artificial intelligence data centers in space could prove easier than on Earth, explaining how aluminum radiators could help future satellites run powerful computers without conventional cooling infrastructure.

Musk Explains How Space Radiators Work

"Yeah, much easier to cool in space," Musk wrote on X, responding to Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire. He estimated that an aluminum radiator facing away from the Sun could release approximately 1,300 watts of heat per square meter because it faces cosmic background radiation at "~3 degrees above absolute zero!"

Unlike Earth’s cooling systems, which often use air or water to carry away heat, spacecraft must release excess heat as invisible infrared radiation. NASA confirms that radiators already perform this function aboard satellites and the International Space Station.

Musk explained that solar panels generate approximately 250 watts of electricity per square meter, meaning satellites would need roughly five times more solar-panel area than radiator area under his assumptions.

"Most of the mass of the satellite is solar panels," he added, reinforcing his earlier argument that orbital AI satellites require relatively simple hardware.

Read Also: Elon Musk's SpaceX Is Preparing a December Stock Gift for Millions of Kids — Trump Accounts to Receive Shares as Another Round of Beneficiaries Gets Added

Starship Could Make Orbital Cooling Practical

Maguire argued that Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) Starship rocket represents the biggest obstacle because launching heavy equipment remains expensive. Once launch costs fall, aluminum structures could transfer heat from computing chips into circulating fluids such as ammonia, allowing radiators to release it into space.

NASA already uses ammonia-based cooling systems aboard the International Space Station, although its main external cooling loops require pumps. SpaceX executives have similarly identified Starship as essential to scaling orbital AI infrastructure.

SpaceX Faces Challenges Scaling Orbital Computing

Reuters reported in June that SpaceX’s proposed first-generation AI satellite could deliver 120 kilowatts of sustained computing power, roughly equivalent to an Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) GB300 server rack. The company plans to adapt existing Starlink technology rather than develop entirely new systems.

However, cooling performance depends on radiator temperature, orientation and exposure to sunlight. Analysts have also questioned whether orbital data centers can overcome launch costs and maintenance challenges.

Elliott Investment Management warned that investors could flip abruptly from the fear of missing out (FOMO) to FOGO, the “fear of getting obliterated.”

In its latest investor letter, as reviewed by The Wall Street Journal, the $80 billion hedge fund led by Paul Singer and Jonathan Pollock compared today’s debt-fueled, tech-heavy markets to the Roaring ’20s before the Great Depression.

“At present, virtually every alarm bell warning of a substantial bear market ahead is ringing,” the letter said.

A Stack of Tail Risks

Elliott flagged widening U.S. budget deficits, persistent inflation, private-credit portfolios and AI hype – including circular investments between tech firms and infrastructure makers, plus debt-financed capital spending.

It also called out zero-day options and meme-stock betting, which it said were more like gambling than investing.

“So many factors have lined up to cause this great boom that it might take disruption in only one or two of them to shift this momentum into reverse,” the firm wrote, warning of “a cascading, self-reinforcing unwind of this bull market.”

The Price of Protection

Elliot’s performance reflects these concerns. It went flat in the third quarter and up a little under 2% through September. In contrast, the S&P 500 returned nearly 13% over the same period.

Distressed debt and hedges tied to gold, currencies, stocks and interest rates lost money. Commodities, arbitrage and credit hedges made money.

“Over Elliott’s five-decade existence, fallow periods have existed, but these have historically been accompanied by market turbulence and followed by periods of rare opportunities,” the letter said.

“Our goal is to be well positioned—protected on the downside, and with capital to deploy into the bargains—when the tide turns again.”

The firm sees opportunities in healthcare activism, producing energy properties and, eventually, forced sellers in dislocated credit markets.

Elliott’s latest 13F filing dated August 14 shows the firm’s lean on hard assets. Triple Flag Precious Metals Corp. (NYSE:TFPM) led at $3.99 billion, 18% of the total.

Phillips 66 (NYSE:PSX) followed at $3.25 billion, then Suncor Energy Inc. (NYSE:SU) at $1.58 billion and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. (NYSE:HPE) at $1.46 billion.

Southwest Airlines Co. (NYSE:LUV), where Elliott won a board overhaul in 2024, remains a $1.25 billion position. PepsiCo Inc. (NASDAQ:PEP) and Synopsys Inc. (NASDAQ:SNPS) are small stakes, at $173 million and $101 million.

The U.S. expansion reached 78 months through October as third-quarter GDP grew 3.4%, while September real spending stalled. SPY investors face a test of earnings breadth and investment returns; IWM investors must also examine domestic demand, debt repricing and interest coverage.

The Print

The U.S. economic expansion has run for 78 months through October 2026, measured from May 2020, the month after the National Bureau of Economic Research’s last designated trough. NBER has not announced a subsequent peak, although its determinations are retrospective.

Real gross domestic product grew 3.4% annualized in the third quarter, accelerating from 2.2% in the second. September was less convincing: real consumer spending was nearly flat, real disposable income fell 0.3%, and payrolls increased by 29,000.

Those contrasting figures set different tests for the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and the iShares Russell 2000 ETF (NYSE:IWM). For SPY, the question is whether investment and output growth translate into earnings across large companies. For IWM, investors must also assess whether smaller businesses can cover borrowing costs when domestic demand softens.

What The GDP Numbers Establish

The 11 U.S. expansions completed since the October 1949 trough averaged 66.6 months. Four lasted longer than 78 months, reaching 92, 106, 120 and 128 months. A historical average is not an expiration date for the current cycle.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that real final sales to private domestic purchasers increased 4.9% annualized in the third quarter, versus 4.6% in the second. This measure includes consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, but excludes inventories, government spending and net exports.

Overall investment growth reflected both private inventory investment and equipment spending, including information-processing equipment. Inventory accumulation can change subsequent production needs, while equipment investment raises the question of whether capital expenditures eventually generate revenue and cash flow.

For the capitalization-weighted S&P 500, stronger aggregate GDP does not establish that earnings gains are broad across constituents. SPY investors can compare growth in sales and operating cash flow with capital spending, and check whether earnings gains are concentrated among a limited group of companies.

September consumer data complicate the picture. Nominal personal consumption expenditures rose 0.5%, but the PCE price index also rose 0.5%. Inflation-adjusted spending increased less than 0.1%, rounded to 0.0%. Higher nominal sales need not signal stronger real demand.

Why IWM Faces A Different Test

IWM tracks the Russell 2000, where borrowing structures add another variable. Wells Fargo Investment Institute reported on October 27 that floating-rate borrowing represented 40.07% of the Russell 2000’s debt classified by interest-rate type, compared with 8.50% for the S&P 500, using data as of October 13.

These percentages concern debt for which interest-rate type could be classified, not all debt outstanding across either index. They are not measurements of ETF-level interest expense.

The gap nevertheless identifies a financing channel worth examining. Floating-rate debt can reprice as short-term rates change, while fixed-rate debt generally reflects prevailing market conditions when refinanced. If demand weakens while borrowing costs remain high, interest expense can absorb more operating income at affected companies.

September payrolls rose 29,000 following revised changes of minus 10,000 in July and plus 133,000 in August. Their sum implies a third-quarter gain of 152,000. August and September estimates remain preliminary.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the approximate 90% confidence interval for a monthly payroll change at plus or minus 122,000. September’s gain is not statistically distinguishable from zero at that level; this does not establish that employment was unchanged.

What Investors Should Watch Next

For SPY, the next test is whether stronger investment translates into broader earnings, margins and cash-flow growth. Investors can examine capital expenditures against operating cash flow and look beyond index-level earnings totals to their concentration.

For IWM, the parallel test combines sales demand and debt service. Quarterly results can show changes in interest expense relative to EBITDA, refinancing rates, interest coverage and free cash flow. Index-level debt exposure alone cannot establish how each company will fare.

September PCE inflation was 3.6% year over year, while core PCE inflation, excluding food and energy, was 3.1%. On October 28, the Federal Reserve held its policy target at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two dissenters preferring an increase.

October employment is scheduled for November 6, while updated third-quarter GDP and October personal income and spending are scheduled for November 25. Both could change the assessment.

The distinction is in what investors need to verify. SPY raises questions about the breadth and returns of investment-led growth. IWM adds a more immediate test of domestic demand, debt repricing and interest coverage. Neither follows from the expansion’s age alone.

news.content: Meta has put proposed changes to its business terms on hold following significant pushback from publishers and open internet advocates. Critics expressed concern that the new provisions would grant the company overly broad access to content on their websites, potentially allowing for the automated collection of journalism to train artificial intelligence services that compete with the publishers' own offerings. Meta has rejected this interpretation, stating that the update was intended to address its advertising and business services. The company's existing terms will remain in effect while the matter is under review, amid intensifying European scrutiny regarding the proposed changes.
news.headline: Meta Pauses Proposed Business Terms Following Publisher Backlash
news.summary: Meta has suspended updates to its business terms after facing opposition from publishers and internet advocates concerned about automated content collection.
